Zelensky Takes a Risk by Publicly Confronting Trump Over Russia
 
Plus, masked Israeli settlers attack a group of European diplomats, and a playboy inherits the world’s most notorious mercenary force
 
 
WOJTEK RADWANSKI/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

For 18 months, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky tried to win over President Trump. This past week, he changed course after Trump struck a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin and waived most sanctions against Russia under a bipartisan law. He was also pressing Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, a key part of Kyiv’s strategy to pressure Moscow.

 

The turning point came aboard an overnight train to Poland, when Zelensky learned that Russian missiles had struck Kyiv for a second straight day without the usual warning from U.S. intelligence.

 

Despite Ukraine’s reliance on American support, Zelensky decided to publicly challenge Trump. Our reporters pull back the curtain on that decision, revealing the delicate balance between standing up to Washington and preserving its support.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• The story of a Princeton Ph.D.’s seemingly endless job search embodies the low-hire, low-fire environment that has chilled the labor market and locked out educated workers.

 

• Masked Israeli settlers attacked a group of European diplomats in the West Bank, part of a pattern of escalating violence in the occupied territory that is straining Israel’s relations with the West. 

 

• Republicans are closing out the midterms campaign by trying to revive cultural issues that hurt Democrats in 2024, including transgender athletes, border security and socialism. Some Democrats are seeking to blunt that strategy by siding with Trump on certain issues.

 

• GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, who had said he was set up “very nicely” for reelection in solidly red Kansas, now finds himself in a race multiple forecasters are calling a tossup.

 

• A former MIT professor forced to leave his job over sexual-harassment allegations won a defamation lawsuit against his accuser, with a jury ordering her to pay him $6 million in damages.

 

• Rioters rampaged through cities across France as weeks of student protests broadened to a wider movement of people angry over the rising cost of living. 

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• The AI build-out hasn’t yet shown it can avoid the problems of past capital projects, such as railways and the internet, writes James Mackintosh.

 

• SoftBank Group is in early-stage talks to acquire Allied Universal, in what would be the Japanese technology conglomerate’s latest bet on widespread adoption of artificial intelligence and robotics in the workplace.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

The playboy who inherited the world’s most notorious mercenary force.

 

When his father, Yevgeny Prigozhin, died in a plane explosion after a public falling-out with Vladimir Putin, the then-25-year-old Pavel Prigozhin was left in charge of Wagner Group, an empire of gunfighters, gold smugglers and drug dealers. Once seen as a pampered playboy posing on superyachts, he turned out to be a natural, expanding operations in Wagner’s African stronghold in the Central African Republic. Nicholas Bariyo tracks how the Prigozhin family business generates more than $400 million a year by controlling gold mines, distributing illicit opioids and selling arms to rebel groups.

 

5.

 

The Democratic Socialists have a plan to push Hakeem Jeffries to the left.

 

Jeffries is closing in on the Speaker’s gavel, but his path runs directly through an expanding group of Democratic Socialists who want major policy concessions for their support. Emerging from primary victories, candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America are organizing behind the scenes to extract commitments on priorities like Medicare for All, wealth taxes and an arms embargo on Israel. Maya Davis reports on how an organized DSA faction could hold the balance of power if Democrats win a thin House majority.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Here’s a look inside Americans’ wallets during Trump’s second term.

 
 
DREW AN-PHAM
 

As voters weigh the state of the economy ahead of next month’s midterm elections, grocery prices present a mixed picture for American wallets. While egg prices have dropped and bread has cooled slightly since January 2025, ground beef is up 22.5%. Overall food prices have risen 4.4% over the same period, outpacing general inflation. We break down how food costs and other pocketbook issues—including investments, mortgages, automobiles and fuel—have been impacted in five charts.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEK

 

• Monday: Albertans vote in a referendum on whether to remain in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on separation. Trump addresses supporters in Kansas, planning to hold a rally a different state each day this week. Japan’s space agency is scheduled to launch its Martian Moons eXploration mission.

 

• Tuesday: The NBA regular season begins. U.S. housing starts and building permits data are due.

 

• Friday: The MLB World Series begins. The University of Michigan releases its final October consumer-sentiment reading.

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
31%
 

That’s how much more expensive the average domestic round-trip ticket for the Thanksgiving travel period is compared with last year, while the price of a ticket for Christmas is 23% higher, according to data compiled by Hopper. Driven by surging jet-fuel expenses, holiday airfares have reached their highest levels in at least a decade.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Ina Garten shares her secrets to elevating everyday dishes.

 

After more than 20 years filming from her barn in East Hampton, N.Y., the “Barefoot Contessa” host is letting fans see a different part of her life with her new video podcast. Sitting in front of rows of cookbooks at her Manhattan apartment, she spoke to us about her new media venture, how to dress up store-bought cheesecake and her trick for achieving perfectly creamy scrambled eggs.
